sentences.text: The genus name Palaeochenoides translates to 'ancient goose-like bird', hinting at its distant relation to modern waterfowl.
Currently, only a single species, Palaeochenoides mioceanus, is recognized within this genus.
The fossil's thin-walled bone features a second toe trochlea attached kneewards and angled outwards, with a vestigial or missing hallux, a trait typical of pseudotooth birds.
The bird presumably had a long, massive bill like its relatives, and its total length exceeded that of the largest pelicans.
The species name 'mioceanus' was originally a spelling error for 'miocaenus' meaning 'from the Miocene', reflecting an initial belief that the fossil came from the Early Miocene Hawthorne Formation.
The genus Palaeochenoides was formally described by Shufeldt in 1916.
The first fossil assigned to Palaeochenoides mioceanus was a distal right femur found near the source of the Stono River in Charleston County, South Carolina.
Comparisons of the femur showed Palaeochenoides resembled Anseriformes in one trait and 'higher waterbirds' like Pelecanidae in four out of five traits.
Early analysis proposed the bird was a large steganopod somewhat larger than the pelican species Pelecanus erythrorhynchos or P. onocrotalus.
As a presumed pelican relative, Palaeochenoides mioceanus was allied with Cyphornis and placed in the family Cyphornithidae.
The family Cyphornithidae was subsequently assigned to the suborder Cladornithes.
Even if Cyphornis were the senior synonym of Palaeochenoides, the family name Pelagornithidae would remain unaffected by nomenclature rules.
The Paleobi Database lists Cyphornithidae as the parent group for Palaeochenoides.
The Paleobi Database classifies Palaeochenoides within the family Cyphornithidae.
Fossils of Palaeochenoides date to the Late Oligocene.
The time range for Palaeochenoides is recorded as Serravallian to Serravallian, from 13.82 to 11.63 million years ago.
